header.title: 🔬 Reflection and refraction simulator
header.subtitle: Explore how light behaves at the boundary between two media

lawReflection.title: Law of reflection
lawReflection.explain: The angle of reflection equals the angle of incidence.

lawSnell.title: Snell’s law (refraction)
lawSnell.explain: Relates the angles and refractive indices in the two media.

critical.title: Critical angle
critical.explain: Minimum angle for total internal reflection (when n₁ > n₂).

rainbow.title: Rainbows
rainbow.body: Rainbows form from refraction and reflection of sunlight in atmospheric water droplets. Each colour has a slightly different refractive index, which produces spectral separation.

diamond.title: Diamond sparkle
diamond.body: Diamond has one of the highest refractive indices (n = 2.42), giving frequent total internal reflection and its characteristic brilliance.

fiber.title: Optical fibre
fiber.body: Optical fibres use total internal reflection to guide light over long distances with little loss. Modern internet relies heavily on this technology.

pool.title: Pools look shallower
pool.body: When you look into water, objects appear closer to the surface than they really are, due to refraction as light passes from water to air.

mirage.title: Mirages
mirage.body: Desert mirages come from refraction in air layers at different temperatures. Hot air near the ground has a lower refractive index.

glasses.title: Spectacle lenses
glasses.body: Glasses correct vision using refraction: converging lenses (for hyperopia) and diverging lenses (for myopia) steer light to focus correctly on the retina.

tech.indexBody: Refractive index (n) is the ratio of the speed of light in vacuum to the speed in a given medium. The larger n, the slower light travels in that medium.
tech.tirBody: When light goes from a denser medium (larger n) to a less dense one and the incidence angle exceeds the critical angle, all light is reflected back into the first medium.
tech.dispersionBody: Refractive index varies slightly with wavelength. Blue light (smaller λ) refracts more than red (larger λ). This is called dispersion.

footer.line2: Based on Snell’s laws and geometrical optics

tips.text: Feather vs hammer — In air the feather drifts slowly because drag is huge. In vacuum (slider at 0) both fall IDENTICALLY — as on the Apollo 15 Moon demo.
Flat vs crumpled paper — Same mass, different shape! The flat sheet has much larger area, so air slows it enormously. Crumpled falls almost like a ball.
Tennis vs bowling ball — Similar spheres but very different mass. The bowling ball hits the ground much sooner in air, though in vacuum they would fall together.
Coin vs feather — Dramatic in air! The coin slices through with tiny area while the feather is braked heavily. Compare terminal speeds!
Basketball vs steel ball — The basketball is heavier but its huge area yields a surprisingly low terminal speed. The steel ball falls much faster.
Brick vs feather — Extreme contrast! The brick is barely affected by air (~48 m/s terminal speed) while the feather floats near ~3 m/s.

header.title: Quantum tunnelling
header.tagline: The electron is not a classical particle — it is a probability wave.

theoryLeft.title: Probability wave, not a trajectory
theoryLeft.p1a: In quantum mechanics, the electron is not a ball with well-defined position and speed before measurement. It is described by a
theoryLeft.p1b: \(\psi(x,t)\), a complex quantity that evolves according to the Schrödinger equation.
theoryLeft.p2a: Born’s rule: the probability of finding the particle between \(a\) and \(b\) is \(P(a \le x \le b) = \int_a^b |\psi(x,t)|^2 \, dx\).
theoryLeft.p2b: is \(\rho(x,t) = |\psi|^2\). In the simulation, the violet “mist” shows \(|\psi|^2\) (discretely normalised on the grid).
theoryLeft.p3b: localises \(\psi\) in space and propagates as a group; the width \(\Delta x\) and momentum \(\Delta p\) obey (in order of magnitude) \(\Delta x\,\Delta p \gtrsim \hbar/2\).
theoryLeft.p4c: slider sets the energy associated with the packet in the demo scale;
theoryLeft.p4d: controls the height \(V\). The ratio \(E/V\) decides whether tunnelling or “going over” dominates.

theoryRight.title: Tunnelling, reflection and transmission
theoryRight.p1a: , if \(E \lt V\), a particle with energy \(E\) would not pass over the barrier.
theoryRight.p1b: , in the region \(V(x) > E\) the solution has an
theoryRight.p2b: the barrier and, after width \(a\), can emerge beyond it with transmission probability \(T\) (tunnelling). For \(E > V\) inside the barrier, the wave is oscillatory (\(\sim e^{\pm i k' x}\)); at interfaces there is
theoryRight.p3b: of height \(V_0\) and width \(a\), with \(E \lt V_0\), transmission decreases roughly exponentially with \(\kappa a\): \(T \sim e^{-2\kappa a}\) (order of magnitude; prefactors depend on details). In the simulation, \(R\) and \(T\) are simplified analytical models.
theoryRight.caption: for \(E \gt V_0\) (rectangular barrier).
theoryRight.note: The visualisation is educational; exact coefficients follow from matching \(\psi\) and \(\mathrm{d}\psi/\mathrm{d}x\) at the barrier edges.

mathAria.rectangular: Rectangular barrier with E greater than V₀

modes.below: The electron tunnels through the barrier: the wave enters the classically forbidden region and a reduced amplitude appears beyond it.
modes.above: The electron passes classically over the barrier (energy above the potential); reflection and transmission oscillate with barrier width.
modes.equal: At the limit E = V, between tunnelling and propagation over the barrier, the coefficients depend sensitively on geometry.

info.intro: This simulator shows the double-slit experiment in the quantum regime. Particles (electrons or photons) do not have an exact position; they are described by a wavefunction that gives the probability of detection.
info.waveP: The wave is not “matter”, but information about where the particle might appear. Brighter regions mean higher probability.
info.interferenceP: When the wave passes through two slits it interferes with itself. That produces high- and low-probability fringes.
info.detectorP: When the detector is on, we learn which slit was used. That destroys interference and the pattern becomes classical: two simple bands.
info.colorsP: The heat map shows probability (ψ²): red = high probability, blue = low.
info.whyP: This phenomenon is central to quantum physics and underpins electrons in atoms, chemical bonding, and much of modern technology.
info.try1: Turn the detector off → see interference
info.try2: Turn the detector on → fringes disappear
info.try4: Increase slit separation → fringes move closer together

page.eyebrow: Heavy water (D₂O vs H₂O) | Interactive simulation

hook.a: What happens if you drink heavy water?
hook.b: Can water shut down a nuclear reactor?
hook.tease: H₂O and D₂O share the same chemical skeleton, but different nuclear masses: deuterium (²H) is almost twice as heavy as protium (¹H). That is why differences show up in biology (isotope exchange), in reactors (neutron capture) and in spectra (vibration frequencies). Pick a mode below.

bonus.p1: Dorel Mihai Constantinescu (b. 1947, Râmnicu Vâlcea) is the Romanian physicist associated with the period when Romania developed its own heavy-water facilities. In the 1970s, at the G plant in Râmnicu Vâlcea, he led the computing laboratory that modelled isotope separation processes and helped obtain the first quantities of D₂O in experimental flow. He also worked on design linked to the complex at Drobeta-Turnu Severin, an important node in the national heavy-water chain.
bonus.p2: In 1976 he was recognised as inventor for a deuterium separation plant using isotope exchange; in 1977 he received a PhD in physics, and in 1981 the Romanian Academy awarded him the Dragomir Hurmuzescu prize. He published on the history of technology in Râmnicu Vâlcea, documenting the experience of a generation of specialists in the nuclear field.

body.desc1: In organisms, water acts as a solvent and as a hydrogen source in enzymatic reactions. D₂O has properties similar to H₂O, but O–D bonds are “heavier” than O–H: some reaction rates drop (kinetic isotope effect), and very high D₂O fractions cause serious physiological effects. In natural water, deuterium is present at about 140 ppm (roughly 0.014% of hydrogen atoms, i.e. about one D per ~7000 H).
body.desc2: The slider sets a fictitious molar fraction of D₂O in a model liquid; the cell grid is for visual intuition only, not a diagnosis.
body.disclaimer2: Educational demo. Do not drink heavy water.

story.vlow: Very low value, close to the natural deuterium background in water (~140 ppm). In the model, the visual effect is essentially zero.
story.low: Low fraction: almost all molecules are still H₂O; in reality, organisms tolerate trace D₂O without obvious effects.
story.mid: Moderate fraction: in the model, the D₂O share increases; in animal experiments, moderate D₂O fractions affect rates of some hydrogen-dependent reactions.
story.high: High fraction: real toxicity rises with dose; in humans, large body fractions of D₂O are dangerous
story.vhigh: Very high fraction: an extreme scenario for on-screen demonstration only.
story.max: 100%: the maximum in the model. In reality, massive D₂O exposure is not something to test — it is harmful.

reactor.desc1: Fission releases very energetic (“fast”) neutrons. To use them efficiently in fuel rods, they must be slowed to thermal energies — called moderation. Molecules around the fuel (heavy or light water) collide with neutrons and reduce their energy.
reactor.fact1: CANDU reactors (e.g. Cernavodă): D₂O moderator, often natural uranium fuel.
reactor.fact2: With H₂O, capture on hydrogen is higher; many designs use enriched fuel instead.
reactor.hintD2o: D₂O: small capture cross section on deuterium; neutrons lose energy via elastic collisions and remain available for fission in the fuel (simplified model).
reactor.hintH2o: H₂O: hydrogen absorbs thermal neutrons in the moderator; fewer neutrons reach the fuel — many light-water reactors use enriched uranium.
reactor.fateD2o: D₂O moderator: small neutron losses in the water; in CANDU design, the chain can be sustained with natural uranium (~0.7% ²³⁵U).
reactor.fateH2o: H₂O moderator: larger losses on hydrogen; in this model the chain thins — in practice this is compensated with enriched fuel or other measures.

physics.panelTitle: H₂O and D₂O: same geometry, different mass
physics.intro: The water molecule has an H–O–H angle of about 104.5°. Replacing ¹H with ²H increases molecular mass by over 10%, while geometry stays similar. Infrared and Raman spectra show lower vibration frequencies for D₂O; as a liquid, D₂O is denser and boils slightly above 100 °C at standard atmospheric pressure.
physics.abundP: Natural deuterium: ~140 ppm (~0.014%) of hydrogen; ordinary water contains only traces of D₂O.
physics.radioP: Ordinary D₂O is not radioactive; tritium (³H) is a different isotope, present only in traces.
physics.thermoP: At standard pressure, D₂O boils near ~101.4 °C — slightly above H₂O — because of bonding and higher mass (hydrogen-bond picture).
physics.massExpP: For a simple harmonic oscillator, a mode frequency depends on reduced mass μ: f ∝ 1 / √μ. In D₂O, μ is larger than in H₂O for similar motions, so characteristic frequencies are lower. The slider tweaks a simplified μ ratio between D₂O and H₂O.
physics.densityP: At the same temperature, one litre of D₂O weighs ~11% more than one litre of H₂O — relevant to isotope separation and industry.
physics.quizQ1: 1. At 1 atm, which boils at the higher temperature?
physics.quizQ2: 2. In CANDU design with natural uranium, the typical moderator is:
physics.quiz1ok: At atmospheric pressure, D₂O boils near ~101.4 °C, slightly above H₂O (100 °C), because of bonding and mass.
physics.quiz1bad: D₂O has a higher boiling point than H₂O at the same pressure.
physics.quiz2ok: Natural-uranium CANDU reactors use a D₂O moderator to limit neutron losses.
physics.quiz2bad: Hydrogen capture in H₂O is high; classic CANDU does not use light-water moderator with natural uranium.

header.title: Full simulation of the Michelson–Morley experiment
header.desc: Explore the interferometer, rotation, fringes and the (hypothetical) ether effect. Adjust every physical parameter to see how the interference pattern changes.

theory.title: Theory and calculations — Michelson–Morley
theory.p1: The interferometer compares travel times along two perpendicular arms. In the classical ether picture, the time difference between arms after a 90° rotation is about Δt ≈ 2 L v² / c³, and the maximum fringe shift on rotation is ΔN ≈ 2 L v² / (λ c²). The phase is Δφ = 2π ΔN.
theory.note: Historically the result was null (no fringe shift was seen), which helped lead to special relativity.

hero.title: Fission simulator
hero.subtitle: Watch how a single neutron starts a chain reaction in uranium-235.

info.title: How it works
info.p1: A slow neutron hits a U-235 nucleus, forming unstable U-236. The nucleus splits into smaller fragments and releases 2–3 new neutrons, plus about 200 MeV of energy.
info.p2: If fuel density exceeds critical mass, the reaction becomes self-sustaining and the k factor rises above 1.
info.tip: Click anywhere on the reactor to launch a neutron.

theoryTab.whatIsP: Circular polarization is a state in which the electric field vector of an electromagnetic wave rotates in a circle as the wave propagates. The tip of the electric field traces a helix in space.
theoryTab.rcpP: The electric field rotates clockwise when viewed facing the propagation direction. Phase difference δ = +90° (π/2).
theoryTab.lcpP: The electric field rotates counter-clockwise when viewed facing the propagation direction. Phase difference δ = −90° (−π/2).
theoryTab.linP: The electric field oscillates in a single plane. Phase difference δ = 0° or 180°.
theoryTab.ellP: The general case where the electric field traces an ellipse. It occurs when the components have different amplitudes or a phase difference other than 90°.
theoryTab.mathIntro: For a wave propagating along z:

advancedTab.jonesCalcP: Jones calculus is a mathematical formalism for polarized light using complex 2×1 Jones vectors and complex 2×2 Jones matrices.
advancedTab.stokesP: Stokes parameters give a complete description of polarization, including partially polarized light.
advancedTab.poincareP: The Poincaré sphere is a graphical representation of all possible polarization states. Points on the sphere represent fully polarized light:
advancedTab.appComP: Satellite communications often use circular polarization
advancedTab.app3dP: RealD 3D uses circular polarization for stereoscopic projection
advancedTab.appRadP: Detecting polarized emission from celestial sources
advancedTab.appNatP: Some animals can detect circularly polarized light
advancedTab.qwP: Converts linear to circular polarization and vice versa. Introduces a 90° phase shift between orthogonal components.
advancedTab.hwP: Rotates the plane of linear polarization. Converts RCP to LCP and vice versa.
advancedTab.polP: Transmits only one linear polarization component, blocking the orthogonal component.

aria.canvas: Interactive sky: constellations, zodiac patterns, and Venus

constelatii.zodiacHook: Newspaper horoscopes use the “tropical” zodiac. Here you see astronomers’ constellations in the real sky—same sky, different story.

venus.title: Venus · the bright “star”
venus.myth: It isn’t a star. It’s the planet Venus.
venus.find: It is the brightest “star” in our sky after the Sun and Moon: look west after sunset or east before sunrise. Thick sulfuric-acid clouds make it shine white; near the horizon it looks more yellow-orange. Its place along the zodiac changes month to month—it’s a planet, not a fixed point like the stars.

uma.title: Big Dipper · Ursa Major
uma.myth: In Greek myth the nymph Callisto was turned into a bear; Zeus placed her in the sky for protection. Nearby is her son Arcas— the Little Dipper. Both “circle forever”, as a reminder of love and punishment.
uma.find: Look for a large dipper pattern. On the short side of the “bowl”, Merak and Dubhe point north: the golden line on the dome runs Merak → Dubhe → Polaris—the same path you extend about five times to reach the North Star and true north.

umi.title: Little Dipper · Ursa Minor
umi.myth: The Little Dipper shares the same tale: Arcas, Callisto’s son, placed in the sky to stay close to his mother. Together the two dippers are the “bears” guarding the north celestial pole.
umi.find: It looks like a smaller dipper around the North Star. Usually you find it after the Big Dipper, following the Dubhe–Merak line toward Polaris; the other stars chain from the handle that ends at Polaris.

polaris.title: Polaris · North Star
polaris.myth: Polaris has guided navigators for millennia: it seems fixed while the rest of the sky wheels around it. In Romanian folklore it was often called the “tailed star”—like a stake pinned high in the sky.
polaris.find: It marks the end of the Little Dipper’s handle, very near the north celestial pole: the whole sky seems to rotate around it. It isn’t the brightest star, but you can find it easily starting from the Big Dipper.

aries.title: Aries · The Ram
aries.myth: The golden ram of the Phrixus and Helle tale, later sacrificed; Zeus set it in the sky as a memorial of courage (and of a trick with golden fleece).
aries.find: Along the ecliptic east of the Pisces–Aries “saddle”; Hamal shines with an orange tint.

taurus.title: Taurus · The Bull
taurus.myth: Zeus became a bull to carry off Europa; in another tale the bull is the quarry of Heracles. Aldebaran glimmers like the beast’s ruddy eye.
taurus.find: In summer and autumn, watch Venus near the same arc as Aldebaran and the Hyades. Elnath marks bright horns toward Gemini.

gemini.title: Gemini · The Twins
gemini.myth: Castor and Pollux, Leda’s sons: one mortal, one immortal, sharing one name in the sky—twins who stay inseparable even as stars.
gemini.find: Two bright stars close together—Castor and Pollux—unmissable on the spring sky.

cancer.title: Cancer · The Crab
cancer.myth: The crab bit Heracles’ foot during his fight with the Hydra—a small pinch, punished with a place in the sky.
cancer.find: A faint pattern between Gemini and Leo; the Beehive cluster (Praesepe) lies near the donkey stars.

leo.title: Leo · The Lion
leo.myth: Heracles’ first labour, the Nemean lion; in the sky Regulus is the beast’s heart; the slain monster becomes the sickle asterism.
leo.find: Regulus sits on the ecliptic; Leo’s “sickle” curls up the lion’s head, then the line drops toward Denebola.

virgo.title: Virgo · The Maiden
virgo.myth: Demeter / Astraea, the last immortal to leave Earth—or the maiden with the ear of grain; Spica is the shining wheat.
virgo.find: Spica is one of the brightest in the figure; it rises in the southeast on spring evenings after Aries sets.

libra.title: Libra · The Scales
libra.myth: The Scorpion’s claws made into scales; goddess Themis and cosmic justice—Libra is the only zodiac sign that is an object, not a creature.
libra.find: Two bright stars, relics of the Scorpion’s old claws; between Virgo and Antares.

scorpius.title: Scorpius · The Scorpion
scorpius.myth: Boastful Orion, stung by a scorpion sent by Artemis; in the sky hunter and beast are kept forever apart.
scorpius.find: Antares, the red “heart”, is a fixed summer landmark; the tail bent south draws a J.

sagittarius.title: Sagittarius · The Archer
sagittarius.myth: The centaur Chiron, gentle teacher, wounded by a poisoned arrow; in the sky he holds his bow toward the Scorpion’s heart.
sagittarius.find: The “Teapot” asterism is easy on the summer Milky Way.

capricornus.title: Capricornus · The Sea-Goat
capricornus.myth: Pan’s goat-fish, who jumped into the Nile with a fish tail to flee Typhon—half goat, half fish.
capricornus.find: South on the ecliptic after Sagittarius; Deneb Algedi’s triangle climbs in late autumn.

aquarius.title: Aquarius · The Water-Bearer
aquarius.myth: Ganymede, cup-bearer of the gods; Aquarius pours water from a celestial jar; the constellation marks blessed rain.
aquarius.find: Sadalmelik and Sadalsuud on the celestial equator; rises autumn through winter near Pisces.

pisces.title: Pisces · The Fish
pisces.myth: Aphrodite and Eros tied with cord to escape Typhon; the two braided fish became a symbol of rising from the waters.
pisces.find: A pale chain on the ecliptic west of Andromeda’s W; Alresha gleams toward the Pisces–Andromeda knot.

header.title: Electromagnetic spectrum
header.subtitle: Interactive simulation — from radio waves to gamma rays

panels.selectHint: Select a band in the spectrum for details.

radio.name: RADIO WAVES
radio.desc: Radio waves have the longest wavelengths in the electromagnetic spectrum. They travel at the speed of light and can cross thousands of kilometres, reflecting from Earth's ionosphere.

microwave.name: MICROWAVES
microwave.range: λ = 1 mm – 1 m · f = 300 MHz – 300 GHz
microwave.desc: Microwaves are used in microwave ovens through resonance of water molecules. They underpin 5G technology and are used to study the cosmos via the cosmic microwave background (CMB).

ir.name: INFRARED
ir.range: λ = 700 nm – 1 mm · f = 300 GHz – 430 THz
ir.desc: Infrared radiation is perceived as heat by the human body. Any object above 0 K emits IR. Thermal cameras can resolve temperature differences down to about 0.01 °C.

visible.name: VISIBLE LIGHT
visible.desc: Visible light is the only part of the electromagnetic spectrum the human eye can detect. Rainbow colours correspond to different frequencies of visible light. Visible lasers are widely used in medicine and industry.

uv.name: ULTRAVIOLET
uv.desc: UV radiation is produced by the Sun and UV lamps. Invisible to the eye, UV-A tans skin, UV-B produces vitamin D but also sunburn, while UV-C (mostly blocked by ozone) is lethal to microbes.

xray.name: X-RAYS
xray.desc: X-rays penetrate soft tissue but are blocked by bone and metal, which makes them indispensable in medicine. Discovered by Wilhelm Röntgen in 1895, they revolutionised diagnosis. At high energies they are used in crystallography and astronomy.

gamma.name: GAMMA RAYS
gamma.desc: Gamma rays are the most energetic radiation in the Universe, produced in nuclear explosions, radioactive decay, and neutron-star collisions (kilonovae). They penetrate almost anything and are lethal in high doses, yet are essential in cancer radiotherapy.

overlay.title: Primary enrichment: up to 30% D₂O across three stages
overlay.p1: Start from 140 ppm (deuterium in natural water).
overlay.p2: Stage 1 brings the mixture to 5%; Stage 2 then unlocks (up to 20%), then Stage 3 — a hypothetical “floodgate break” — up to 30%.

3.name: Stage 3
3.hypothesis: Hypothetical scenario (unbuilt plan): extra liquid circulation between columns.
3.rupereRest: in an isotopic-separation cascade, past a concentration threshold the design optimum changes (different flow ratio, different number of equivalent stages). This is an imaginary exercise: two extra liquid bypasses between columns so you can see how behaviour “breaks away” from the classic stages — not a 1:1 match to any real plant floor.

success.title: Congratulations! You completed all three stages.
success.body: You reached the 30% D₂O target in the hypothetical “floodgate break” stage.
success.summaryP1: You raised the concentration from 140 ppm to 30% D₂O, moving through the isotopic-exchange stages in turn.
success.summaryP2: Stage 1: up to 5% with the cold column at {cold}°C, the hot column at {hot}°C, and L/G {lg}.
success.summaryP4: Stage 3: the hypothetical “floodgate break” scenario up to 30% — with extra liquid bypasses only as a design idea, not as a documented real installation here.

panel.hintInitial: Select an unlocked stage on the left. Stage 1 goes up to 5%; then Stage 2 unlocks (up to 20%), then Stage 3 (hypothesis, up to 30%).
panel.noteText: Vacuum distillation is not part of this exercise — that is a separate process step. All three stages here use the same H₂O–H₂S model; Stage 3 only adds the hypothetical visual with extra liquid ties.

hints.etaj1: Target: 5% D₂O. Set L/G between 0.48–0.52 (ideal 0.50), cold column ~35°C and hot ~130°C. At 5%, Stage 2 unlocks and you switch to it automatically.
hints.etaj2: Target: 20% D₂O. Same parameters as stage 1. At 20%, Stage 3 unlocks and you switch automatically (“floodgate break” scenario).
hints.etaj2b: Target: 20% D₂O. You reached 20% — Stage 3 (hypothesis) is active. Continue toward 30%.
hints.etaj3: Target: 30% D₂O — “floodgate break”. Hypothetical stage: visually there are also liquid ties between columns (unbuilt plan). Parameters stay the same as stages 1–2.

info.title: Quick facts · the four isotopes that matter

sim.title: Nucleus simulator
sim.lead: Switch isotope, inspect the N/Z ratio, trigger an α decay.

lab.title: WOW module · Fission & time
lab.lead: Things break apart here. Hit U‑235 with a neutron, or run billions of years in the sim.

fission.cardLead: A slow neutron hits the nucleus → fragments + 2–3 neutrons + energy.
fission.massEnergyHint: The mass difference becomes energy. ~200 MeV per fission.

compare.cardLead: Why is one fuel and the other not?

timeMachine.title: ⏳ Time machine · radioactive decay
timeMachine.lead: 1000 atoms. Press Start and watch them vanish over time. Exponential decay: N(t) = N₀·(½)^(t/T½).

theory.sectionLead: Quick reference for the nucleus, α decay and the time module; details and the Formulas tab on the site.
theory.li1Html: Notation: A = Z + N — for uranium, Z = 92.
theory.li2Html: α decay: the nucleus emits ⁴₂He; the daughter has Z − 2, A − 4.
theory.li3Html: Radioactivity: N(t) = N₀·e−λt, λ = ln(2)/T½ (same structure as the “all isotopes” chart).

decay.defaultNoteHtml: In α decay: AZX → A−4Z−2Y + 42He. Example: 23592U → 23190Th + α.

U-233.desc: Produced from thorium‑232. Fissile like U‑235; studied for generation‑IV concepts.

U-234.desc: Appears from U‑238 decay (≈0.0055% of natural uranium). Minor industrial role.

U-235.desc: The only naturally occurring isotope fissile with thermal neutrons. ~0.72% of natural U. Reactor and weapons fuel.

U-238.desc: >99% of natural uranium. Not fissile with thermal neutrons, but can capture a neutron and breed Pu‑239 (fissile).

hero.subtitle: 26 isotopes, from microseconds to billions of years. Same nucleus, always 92 protons — only the neutrons change everything.

timeline.h2: From discovery to the nuclide map

y1789.p: Martin Heinrich Klaproth isolates uranium from pitchblende and names it after the planet Uranus.

y1896.p: Henri Becquerel observes spontaneous radiation from uranium salts. A new science is born.

y1913.p: Frederick Soddy shows that atoms of one element can have different masses. Uranium would have dozens.

y1938.p: Hahn & Strassmann split the nucleus. U-235 becomes the most important industrial isotope in history.

today.p: From U-217 (26 ms) to U-242 (~17 min). Only three occur in nature: U-234, U-235, U-238.

chart.lead: Each cell is one isotope. Color = decay type. Brightness = relative stability. Click or navigate.

explorer.lead: Move the slider or tap a cell above.

decay.leadAfter: Same formula for every isotope — only λ changes.

theory.lead: The same Z = 92 for all isotopes; N and A differ. Stability and decay mode depend on distance from the “valley of stability”.
theory.li2Html: Radioactive decay: N(t) = N₀·e−λt, λ = ln(2)/T½ — used in the panel when you pick an isotope.
theory.li3Html: Natural isotopes: typical rock/ore is dominated by U-238 (~99.3%), U-235 (~0.72%), with U-234 as a trace in the U-238 chain.

footer.note: Data are current estimates for experimentally known uranium isotopes (A = 217 → 242).

217.desc: A very light uranium isotope made in accelerators. Gone in tens of milliseconds.

218.desc: Among the least stable isotopes: the atom lasts less than a millisecond.

219.desc: Sub‑millisecond lifetime. Studied for nuclear structure of the lightest U isotopes.

220.desc: Estimated value. Essentially instantaneous — decay in tens of nanoseconds.

221.desc: Produced in heavy‑ion reactions. Lifetime on the scale of a laser flash.

222.desc: Estimated. Probes the fission barrier for very light U isotopes.

223.desc: Ultra‑short lifetime. Detected via α‑particle spectroscopy.

224.desc: Millisecond scale — among the first U isotopes with ms‑scale lifetimes.

225.desc: Under a tenth of a second. Used in short α‑decay chain studies.

226.desc: Lasts a moment. Useful marker in decay‑chain experiments.

227.desc: About a minute of existence. Produced in controlled nuclear reactions.

228.desc: As A increases, lifetime tends to grow — tied to nuclear binding trends.

229.desc: First U isotope decaying mainly by electron capture rather than α.

230.desc: Studied as a potential α‑therapy agent. Lives almost three weeks.

231.desc: A few days’ lifetime. Intermediate in artificial decay chains.

232.desc: Appears in the Th–U cycle. Problematic: strong γ rays via its progeny.

233.desc: Fissile like U‑235. Breeds from Th‑232 via neutron capture — Generation‑IV interest.

234.desc: Natural daughter of U‑238 decay. Only ~55 ppm of natural uranium.

235.desc: The only naturally occurring thermal‑neutron fissile isotope. Main reactor fuel.

236.desc: Neutron‑irradiation marker. In pristine samples → hint of nuclear processing.

237.desc: Reactor product. Used to trace plutonium production pathways. β⁻ to neptunium.

238.desc: >99% of Earth’s uranium. Not thermal‑fissile, but captures neutrons to breed fissile Pu‑239.

239.desc: Key link: U‑238 + n → U‑239 → Np‑239 → Pu‑239 — how plutonium is made.

240.desc: From multiple neutron capture in reactors.

242.desc: Heaviest uranium isotope observed experimentally; beyond lies mostly theory.

header.title: Fractional distillation H₂O – D₂O
header.tagline: After isotopic exchange (~20% D₂O) — fine separation by boiling points · educational model
header.scienceBite: Boiling point gap: ~1.4 °C between H₂O and D₂O — so separation is extremely slow and needs many theoretical stages.

gsLock.p2: simulation through the success screen (~30% D₂O). Only then can you continue with fractional distillation — in practice the GS stage brings concentration into the tens of percent; fine rectification pushes toward nuclear-grade purity.

intro.hook: You brought heavy water to 20%… but the real fight has just begun.
intro.p1: H₂O boils at ~100 °C, D₂O at ~101.4 °C — a small gap, so you need
intro.p2: . One column: condenser on top, reboiler at the bottom; vapours ↑ (richer in H₂O), liquid ↓ (D₂O concentrates at the bottom).

column.topProductHint: light liquid (H₂O) — less D₂O than at the bottom
column.refluxCaption: Reflux: condensed liquid returns to the column
column.refluxDrip: Condensed liquid ↓ back into the column

readouts.tReboilerTip: Too low: little vaporisation, the column “doesn’t work”. Too high: risk of losses / simplified teaching model.
readouts.stagesTip: More equivalent stages = more vapour–liquid contacts. With few stages, separation is slow or weak.
readouts.refluxTip: R = L/D: how much liquid returns to the column vs product taken. In this teaching model R is fixed between 1 and 1.5.
readouts.alphaTip: α close to 1 (e.g. 1.05–1.07) means very hard separation: each stage changes composition only a little, so you need many stages and reflux.

panel.chartNote: X axis: simulated time · Y axis: % D₂O in reboiler liquid. The last percent towards the target are the slowest (plateau) — “the last 5% are hell”.
panel.noteRest: — it shows the role of theoretical stages, reflux, and temperature in rectification with low relative volatility (α close to 1). It does not replace industrial design or real vacuum distillation.
panel.noteExtra: H₂O/D₂O separation is one of the hardest in chemical engineering: very similar properties, so high energy use and very tall equipment for nuclear purity.
panel.alphaHint: With α ≈ 1.066 (H₂O more volatile than D₂O): separation is difficult — you need many theoretical stages and high reflux to approach 99.8% D₂O at the reboiler.

presets.rapidTitle: Few theoretical stages, R = 1 (minimum in the teaching range): fast but weak separation
presets.industrialTitle: Many theoretical stages and R = 1.5 (maximum in the teaching range): path to high purity (slow)

labels.reboilerTempTitle: Below ~100 °C effective vaporisation drops; the reboiler should sit in the H₂O–D₂O window.
labels.stagesTitle: Each theoretical stage corresponds, in the model, to a distillation tray (vapour–liquid contact).
labels.refluxTitle: R between 1 and 1.5 (teaching parameters): higher values return more liquid to the column.

process.boilLow: Temperature too low: no efficient vaporisation in the reboiler.
process.phase1: H₂O evaporates preferentially — vapour richer in light water rises toward the condenser.
process.phase2: Reflux improves separation: liquid returns and washes D₂O toward the column base.
process.phase3: Near maximum purity → slow process (plateau). The last percent are the most expensive.
process.phase4: Teaching target reached in the model — in practice the last ppm need more time and stages.

distilare-d2o-fractionata.tempWarning: Little vaporisation at this temperature — raise the reboiler slightly.

descriptions.semiconductor: Orbitals align like in a network, while transfer stays energetically controlled.
descriptions.metallic: Electrons delocalise and flow through a shared electron-like cloud.
descriptions.covalent: A bonding electron oscillates between nuclei, and the cloud stays nearly symmetric.
descriptions.polarCovalent: The cloud polarises and electron density shifts toward the more electronegative atom.
descriptions.ionic: Bond formation pushes the electron toward the acceptor and clearly separates donor from acceptor.
